subject: HSS
title: U.S. History & Geography: Continuity and Change in the Twentieth Century
description: Following the California HSS Framework for grade 11, this course briefly reviews the nation's founding and nineteenth-century transformations, then studies the twentieth century in depth: industrialization and Progressivism, America's rise as a world power, the 1920s, the Depression and New Deal, World War II, the Cold War, the civil rights movements, and contemporary America. Students analyze primary sources each week (from the Library of Congress, National Archives/DocsTeach, and Calisphere), write document-based essays, and complete a National History Day–style research project. California's role (immigration, agriculture, Japanese American incarceration, aerospace, the Chicano and farmworker movements) is emphasized throughout.
framework: California History–Social Science Content Standards (Grade 11); 2016 California History–Social Science Framework

standards.11.1: Analyze the significant events in the founding of the nation and its attempts to realize the philosophy of government described in the Declaration of Independence.
standards.11.1.1: Describe the Enlightenment and the rise of democratic ideas as the context in which the nation was founded.
standards.11.1.2: Analyze the ideological origins of the American Revolution, the Founding Fathers' philosophy of divinely bestowed unalienable rights, and the Declaration and Constitution.
standards.11.1.3: Understand the history of the Constitution after 1787 with emphasis on federal versus state authority and growing democratization.
standards.11.1.4: Examine the effects of the Civil War and Reconstruction and of the industrial revolution, including demographic shifts and the emergence of the U.S. as a world power.
standards.11.2: Analyze the relationship among the rise of industrialization, large-scale rural-to-urban migration, and massive immigration from Southern and Eastern Europe.
standards.11.2.1: Know the effects of industrialization on living and working conditions, including the portrayal of working conditions and food safety in Sinclair's The Jungle.
standards.11.2.2: Describe the changing landscape, including the growth of cities linked by industry and trade, and the development of cities divided by race, ethnicity, and class.
standards.11.2.3: Trace the effect of the Americanization movement.
standards.11.2.4: Analyze the effect of urban political machines and responses to them by immigrants and middle-class reformers.
standards.11.2.5: Discuss corporate mergers that produced trusts and cartels and the economic and political policies of industrial leaders.
standards.11.2.6: Trace the economic development of the U.S. and its emergence as a major industrial power, including its gains from trade and advantages of its physical geography.
standards.11.2.7: Analyze the similarities and differences between the ideologies of Social Darwinism and Social Gospel.
standards.11.2.8: Examine the effect of political programs and activities of Populists.
standards.11.2.9: Understand the effect of political programs and activities of the Progressives (federal regulation, Roosevelt, Wilson, women's suffrage).
standards.11.3: Students analyze the role religion played in the founding of America, its lasting moral, social, and political impacts, and issues regarding religious liberty.
standards.11.3.2: Analyze the great religious revivals and the leaders involved in them, including the First and Second Great Awakenings and the Civil War revivals.
standards.11.3.5: Describe the principles of religious liberty found in the Establishment and Free Exercise clauses of the First Amendment.
standards.11.4: Trace the rise of the United States to its role as a world power in the twentieth century.
standards.11.4.1: List the purpose and the effects of the Open Door policy.
standards.11.4.2: Describe the Spanish-American War and U.S. expansion in the South Pacific.
standards.11.4.3: Discuss America's role in the Panama Revolution and the building of the Panama Canal.
standards.11.4.4: Explain Theodore Roosevelt's Big Stick diplomacy, William Taft's Dollar Diplomacy, and Woodrow Wilson's Moral Diplomacy.
standards.11.4.5: Analyze the political, economic, and social ramifications of World War I on the home front.
standards.11.4.6: Trace the declining role of Great Britain and the expanding role of the United States in world affairs after World War II.
standards.11.5: Analyze the major political, social, economic, technological, and cultural developments of the 1920s.
standards.11.5.1: Discuss the policies of Presidents Harding, Coolidge, and Hoover.
standards.11.5.2: Analyze the international and domestic events, interests, and philosophies that prompted attacks on civil liberties, including the Palmer Raids, Marcus Garvey's 'back-to-Africa' movement, the Ku Klux Klan, and immigration quotas.
standards.11.5.3: Examine the passage of the Eighteenth Amendment and the Volstead Act (Prohibition).
standards.11.5.4: Analyze the passage of the Nineteenth Amendment and the changing role of women in society.
standards.11.5.5: Describe the Harlem Renaissance and new trends in literature, music, and art.
standards.11.5.6: Trace the growth and effects of radio and movies and their role in the worldwide diffusion of popular culture.
standards.11.5.7: Discuss the rise of mass production techniques, the growth of cities, the impact of new technologies (the automobile, electricity), and the resulting prosperity and effect on the American landscape.
standards.11.6: Analyze the different explanations for the Great Depression and how the New Deal fundamentally changed the role of the federal government.
standards.11.6.1: Describe the monetary issues of the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries that gave rise to the establishment of the Federal Reserve.
standards.11.6.2: Understand the explanations of the principal causes of the Great Depression and the steps taken by the Federal Reserve, Congress, and Presidents Hoover and Roosevelt.
standards.11.6.3: Discuss the human toll of the Depression, natural disasters, and unwise agricultural practices and their effects on the depopulation of rural regions and political movements of the left and right.
standards.11.6.4: Analyze the effects of and the controversies arising from New Deal economic policies and the expanded role of the federal government.
standards.11.6.5: Trace the advances and retreats of organized labor, from the creation of the AFL and CIO to current issues of a postindustrial, multinational economy.
standards.11.7: Analyze America's participation in World War II.
standards.11.7.1: Examine the origins of American involvement in the war, with an emphasis on the events that precipitated the attack on Pearl Harbor.
standards.11.7.2: Explain U.S. and Allied wartime strategy, including the major battles of Midway, Normandy, Iwo Jima, Okinawa, and the Battle of the Bulge.
standards.11.7.3: Identify the roles and sacrifices of individual American soldiers, as well as the unique contributions of special fighting forces (Tuskegee Airmen, 442nd Regimental Combat Team, Navajo Code Talkers).
standards.11.7.4: Analyze Roosevelt's foreign policy during World War II (e.g., Four Freedoms speech).
standards.11.7.5: Discuss the constitutional issues and impact of events on the U.S. home front, including the internment of Japanese Americans, restrictions on German and Italian resident aliens, and the response to the Holocaust.
standards.11.7.6: Describe major developments in aviation, weaponry, communication, and medicine and the war's impact on the location of American industry and use of resources.
standards.11.7.7: Discuss the decision to drop atomic bombs and the consequences of the decision.
standards.11.7.8: Analyze the effect of massive aid given to Western Europe under the Marshall Plan to rebuild itself after the war and the importance of a rebuilt Europe to the U.S. economy.
standards.11.8: Analyze the economic boom and social transformation of post–World War II America.
standards.11.8.1: Trace the growth of service sector, white collar, and professional sector jobs in business and government.
standards.11.8.2: Describe the significance of Mexican immigration and its relationship to the agricultural economy, especially in California.
standards.11.8.4: Analyze new federal government spending on defense, welfare, interest on the national debt, and federal and state spending on education, including the California Master Plan.
standards.11.8.6: Discuss the diverse environmental regions of North America, their relationship to local economies, and the origins and prospects of environmental problems.
standards.11.8.7: Describe the effects on society and the economy of technological developments since 1945, including the computer revolution.
standards.11.8.8: Discuss forms of popular culture, with emphasis on their origins and geographic diffusion (e.g., jazz and other forms of popular music, professional sports, architectural and artistic styles).
standards.11.9: Analyze U.S. foreign policy since World War II.
standards.11.9.1: Discuss the establishment of the United Nations and International Declaration of Human Rights, IMF, World Bank, and GATT and their importance in shaping modern Europe and maintaining peace.
standards.11.9.2: Understand the role of military alliances, including NATO and SEATO, in deterring communist aggression and maintaining security during the Cold War.
standards.11.9.3: Trace the origins and geopolitical consequences of the Cold War and containment policy, including the Truman Doctrine, Berlin Blockade, Korean War, Bay of Pigs, Cuban Missile Crisis, Vietnam, and Latin American policy.
standards.11.9.4: List the effects of foreign policy on domestic policies and vice versa (e.g., protests during the war in Vietnam, the 'nuclear freeze' movement).
standards.11.9.5: Analyze the role of the Reagan administration and other factors in the victory of the West in the Cold War.
standards.11.9.6: Describe U.S. Middle East policy and its strategic, political, and economic interests, including those related to the Gulf War.
standards.11.9.7: Examine relations between the United States and Mexico in the twentieth century, including key economic, political, immigration, and environmental issues.
standards.11.10: Analyze the development of federal civil rights and voting rights.
standards.11.10.1: Explain how demands of African Americans helped produce a stimulus for civil rights, including Executive Order 8802 and the desegregation of the armed forces.
standards.11.10.2: Examine and analyze the key events, policies, and court cases in the evolution of civil rights, including Dred Scott, Plessy, Brown, Regents v. Bakke, and California Proposition 209.
standards.11.10.3: Describe the collaboration on legal strategy between African American and white civil rights lawyers to end racial segregation in higher education.
standards.11.10.4: Examine the roles of civil rights advocates (A. Philip Randolph, Martin Luther King Jr., Malcolm X, Thurgood Marshall, James Farmer, Rosa Parks), including 'Letter from Birmingham Jail' and 'I Have a Dream.'
standards.11.10.5: Discuss the diffusion of the civil rights movement of African Americans to the civil rights movements of other groups (Latinos, Asian Americans, Native Americans, women, LGBT Americans, persons with disabilities).
standards.11.10.6: Analyze the passage and effects of civil rights and voting rights legislation (Civil Rights Act of 1964, Voting Rights Acts of 1965) and the Twenty-Fourth Amendment, with emphasis on equality of access to education and the political process.
standards.11.10.7: Analyze the women's rights movement from the era of Elizabeth Stanton and Susan Anthony and the passage of the Nineteenth Amendment to the movement launched in the 1960s, including differing perspectives on the roles of women.
standards.11.11: Analyze the major social problems and domestic policy issues in contemporary American society.
standards.11.11.1: Discuss the reasons for the nation's changing immigration policy, with emphasis on how the Immigration Act of 1965 and successor acts have transformed American society.
standards.11.11.2: Discuss the significant domestic policy speeches of Truman, Eisenhower, Kennedy, Johnson, Nixon, Carter, Reagan, Bush, and Clinton (e.g., education, civil rights, economic policy, environmental policy).
standards.11.11.3: Describe the changing roles of women in society as reflected in the entry of more women into the labor force and the changing family structure.
standards.11.11.4: Explain the constitutional crisis originating from the Watergate scandal.
standards.11.11.5: Trace the impact of, need for, and controversies associated with environmental conservation, expansion of the national park system, and the development of environmental protection laws.
standards.11.11.6: Analyze the persistent big-city problems of the late twentieth century, including the issues of homelessness, crime, and drug abuse.
standards.11.11.7: Explain how the federal, state, and local governments have responded to demographic and social changes such as population shifts to the suburbs, racial concentrations in the cities, Frostbelt-to-Sunbelt migration, international migration, decline of family farms, increases in out-of-wedlock births, and drug abuse.

units.title: Foundations Review: Founding Ideals to Reconstruction
units.big_idea: The founding ideals of liberty and equality set a standard that every later generation measured itself against.

units.title: Industrialization, Immigration, and Urbanization
units.big_idea: Industrial capitalism transformed where and how Americans lived and worked, drawing millions of immigrants to growing cities.

units.title: Progressivism and America as a World Power
units.big_idea: Reformers used government to tame industrial problems while the U.S. expanded its power overseas.

units.title: World War I and the 1920s
units.big_idea: War and prosperity brought new technologies and cultures alongside fierce conflicts over civil liberties and identity.

units.title: The Great Depression and the New Deal
units.big_idea: Economic collapse led Americans to accept a permanently larger role for the federal government.

units.title: World War II
units.big_idea: Total war mobilized every part of American society, tested constitutional rights at home, and made the U.S. a superpower.

units.title: Postwar America and the Cold War
units.big_idea: Fear of communism shaped foreign policy, domestic politics, and a booming consumer society.

units.title: The Civil Rights Movements
units.big_idea: African Americans and other groups used courts, legislation, and nonviolent protest to claim equal citizenship.

units.title: Contemporary America
units.big_idea: Since 1968, Americans have debated the role of government, immigration, the environment, and America's place in the world.

units.title: History Research Project and Final Exam
units.big_idea: Historians build arguments from evidence and must weigh multiple perspectives.

weeks.topic: History research project: question and sources

days.work: Choose a 20th-century topic connected to California and the annual National History Day theme; write a research question.

days.title: Primary sources
days.work: Find at least six primary sources on Calisphere, LOC, or DocsTeach.

days.title: Secondary sources
days.work: Find three secondary sources from library databases and summarize historians' interpretations.

days.title: Annotated bibliography
days.work: Write an annotated bibliography separated into primary and secondary sources.

days.title: Check

weeks.topic: History research project: build and present

days.title: Outline

days.work: Build an exhibit, website, documentary, or 2,000-word paper.

days.work: Write a 500-word process paper.
